description: Phases of the software development lifecycle

screens.body:
The SDLC — software development lifecycle — is the journey software takes from "we have an idea" to "it's live and people use it." It's a set of phases, and each phase hands its work to the next one.

Think of building a house: you wouldn't pour concrete before drawing the floor plan. Software works the same way — skipping ahead is how projects turn into expensive messes.

options: The journey from idea to live software, in phases
check.question: The SDLC is…

screens.heading: What the SDLC is
screens.keyPoint: Idea to live software, one phase at a time.

screens.body:
Most teams use these phases: first you figure out what's needed (requirements), then you plan how to build it (design), then you write the code (implementation), then you check it works (testing), then you release it (deployment), and finally you keep it healthy (maintenance).

The names shift a little between teams, but the order of thinking stays the same: understand → plan → build → verify → release → care for it.

options: Requirements → design → build → test → deploy → maintain
check.question: The usual phase order is…

screens.heading: The phases in order
screens.keyPoint: Understand, plan, build, verify, release, maintain.

screens.body:
Waterfall is the classic approach: finish one phase completely before starting the next, like water flowing down steps. You gather ALL requirements, then do ALL the design, then write ALL the code.

It works best when the requirements are stable and clear up front — like rebuilding a well-understood system. Its weakness: if the client changes their mind late, going back upstream is painful and expensive.

options: Finish each phase fully before the next starts
Build everything in tiny daily loops
check.question: Waterfall means…

screens.heading: Waterfall: the classic
screens.keyPoint: One phase at a time, top to bottom.

screens.body:
Agile and iterative approaches flip that: build a small working slice, show it, get feedback, and loop. Instead of one giant waterfall, you run many small cycles — each one goes through mini phases of plan, build, and test.

This shines when requirements WILL change — which, honestly, is most real projects. The tradeoff: it needs an engaged client and disciplined habits, or the loops drift.

options: Build in small loops with feedback each round
Write all the code in one go
check.question: Agile/iterative means…

screens.heading: Agile: small loops

screens.body:
Software is a team sport. The client (or product owner) brings the need and the money. A business analyst turns that need into clear requirements. Designers plan the structure; developers build it; testers try to break it; and a project manager keeps everyone moving together.

On small projects one person wears several hats — that's you on SwiftGigs, being analyst, designer, developer, and tester all at once. Knowing the roles still helps you switch hats on purpose.

options: Analyst, designer, developer, tester, project manager
The client does all the testing
check.question: Typical SDLC roles include…

screens.heading: Who's on the team
screens.keyPoint: Different hats, one goal: working software.

screens.body:
Here's a bigger idea behind all of this: a system is a set of parts working together toward a goal. Every system has inputs (what goes in), processes (what happens), and outputs (what comes out).

Your app is a system. So is the team building it. So is the business it serves. When you think in systems, you stop fixing one screen and start asking: what feeds into this, and what does it feed?

options: Inputs → processes → outputs, working toward a goal
check.question: A system is…

screens.heading: Thinking in systems
screens.keyPoint: Inputs in, processes happen, outputs out.

screens.body:
Here's the uncomfortable truth: most failed projects didn't fail at coding — they failed at the early phases. Vague requirements and skipped design mean developers build the wrong thing beautifully.

That's why this course front-loads analysis and design. Time spent understanding the problem is the cheapest time in the whole lifecycle. A bug found in requirements costs almost nothing; the same bug found after release costs a fortune.

options: Most failures start in the early phases, not in coding
check.question: Where do most projects actually fail?

screens.heading: Why the early phases matter most
screens.keyPoint: Fix it on paper, not in production.

screens.body: Agile Manifesto (agilemanifesto.org) — the original short statement of agile values, straight from the source. Scrum.org — the official Scrum Guide if you want the most common agile framework. OMG (omg.org) — the standards body behind UML, useful once you start drawing designs.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: Read the Agile Manifesto in its own words.
